sections.label: Community corrections and recidivism figures
sections.summary: Community corrections numbers rose from about 850 in 2011 to over 3,400 in 2021, and the 2018 two-year recidivism rate was 22%.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: With the implementation of these programmes, the number of inmates and ex-offenders on community corrections has increased over the years, from about 850 in 2011 to more than 3,400 in 2021.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The two-year recidivism rate for inmates released in 2018 was 22%, down from 44% two decades ago.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: From 2016 to 2020, 997 inmates were emplaced on the WRS and 90% of them successfully completed the programme.

sections.label: EmPS eligibility conditions
sections.summary: Inmates are eligible for the EmPS if they have served at least 14 days of imprisonment and the Commissioner considers them suitable.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Inmates are eligible for the EmPS if they have served at least 14 days of imprisonment, and the Commissioner considers them suitable for the EmPS.

sections.label: Inmate drug and cost rules
sections.summary: Inmates must not consume controlled drugs, alcohol or intoxicating substances, and clause 26 lets the Minister prescribe regulations for inmates to pay outside costs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Specifically, inmates are not to consume any controlled drug or alcoholic beverage or use or inhale any intoxicating substance or possess any controlled drugs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Second, clause 26 allows the Minister for Home Affairs to prescribe via regulations for inmates on these schemes to pay for the costs of goods and services incurred by them outside prison, such as food, transport and medical treatment.

sections.label: Deferring release for court punishment
sections.summary: Clause 9 allows the Commissioner to defer an inmate's release by up to three weeks to carry out Court-ordered punishment without seeking a Court order.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: From 2017 to 2021, on average, there were nine inmates per year whose release was deferred by the Commissioner under section 50I(3) of the Prisons Act and four inmates per year whose detention was extended by the Court under section 326 of the Criminal Procedure Code in order to carry out any outstanding Court-ordered punishment.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Clause 9 allows the Commissioner to defer an inmate's release by up to three weeks to allow SPS sufficient time to carry out any Court-ordered punishment, without having to seek an order from the Court to extend the inmate's detention.

sections.label: Undertaking before communicating with inmates
sections.summary: The Minister for Home Affairs may make regulations requiring prescribed persons to give an undertaking before communicating with an inmate.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: First, the Minister for Home Affairs may make regulations to require prescribed persons, or prescribed classes of persons to give an undertaking before they are permitted to communicate with an inmate.

sections.label: Redacting inmate correspondence material
sections.summary: The Minister for Home Affairs may make regulations to redact or withhold material in inmates' correspondence that affects prison security or incites an offence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Second, the Minister for Home Affairs may make regulations to redact or withhold any material in inmates' correspondence with any prescribed person, or prescribed classes of persons, that may: first, affect the security or good order of a prison; or second, incite the commission of any offence.

sections.label: Deleted minor prison offences
sections.summary: Clause 24 deletes two minor prison offences: idling or refusing to work or showing negligence, and refusing medical treatment.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: For instance, clause 24 deletes two minor prison offences, "idling or refusing to work or showing negligence in the performance of his allotted task" and "refusing to undergo medical treatment".

sections.label: EmPS and EPS breaches
sections.summary: Clause 24 will also specify prison offences for inmates who breach the conditions of the EmPS and EPS.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Clause 24 will also specify prison offences for inmates who breach the conditions of the EmPS and EPS.

sections.label: Prison officers' inquiry powers
sections.summary: Clause 25 empowers prison officers of and above Sergeant rank to require third parties to provide documents or information for inquiries into breaches and prison offences.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: To bridge this gap, clause 25 empowers prison officers of and above the rank of Sergeant to require third parties to provide documents or information that are necessary for the inquiries into the breaches and prison offences.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Clause 27 inserts a related amendment to the Misuse of Drugs Act, to grant prison officers similar powers to assist them in conducting inquiries into breaches of conditions of community-based programmes by DRC and Community Rehabilitation Centre inmates.

sections.label: Protection from liability
sections.summary: The protection from liability for officers carrying out lawful duties will be made explicit in the Prisons Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: To allow these officers to carry out their lawful duties with greater assurance, we will make this protection from liability explicit in the Prisons Act.

sections.label: Juvenile age limit raised
sections.summary: Clause 2 raises the upper age limit for "juvenile" from below 16 years to below 18 years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Clause 2 updates the definition of "juvenile" by raising the upper age limit from below 16 years to below 18 years, to align it with the updated definition that was passed under the Children and Young Persons (Amendment) Act 2019.

sections.label: SPS recidivism rate
sections.summary: Recidivism reported in SPS' 2020 Annual Report stands at 22.1%, half the recidivism of the early 2000s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: A testimony to the good work that SPS does lies with the fact, as said by the hon Minister of State just now, recidivism reported in SPS’ 2020 Annual Report stands at 22.1% and he mentioned that this is half the recidivism that was the case in the early 2000s.

sections.label: ex-offenders employed through JGI
sections.summary: Almost 800 ex-offenders were employed through JGI between September 2020 and February 2021, and JGI was extended to March 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Between September 2020 and February 2021, a span of six months, almost 800 ex-offenders were employed through JGI.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I am sure many more ex-offenders would have benefited since then from JGI, which was recently extended to March 2022.

sections.label: clause 9 remission order deferral
sections.summary: Clause 9 amends section 50I of the Prisons Act to give the Commissioner three weeks, instead of two, to defer a remission order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Moving on to the other aspects of the Bill, I have a short query on clause 9 of the Bill which proposes to amend the existing section 50I of the Prisons Act such that the Commissioner is given three weeks, instead of the previous two weeks, to defer the making of the remission order.

sections.label: Commissioner conflict of interest remission
sections.summary: The Prisons Act lets SPS restore forfeited remission, which could put the Commissioner in a position of conflict of interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Prisons Act also vests with SPS the power to restore any period of forfeited remission.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We could, therefore, potentially have a situation where the Commissioner is asked to consider deferring the issuance of a remission order because there is insufficient time for the carrying out of corporal punishment on an inmate because of, amongst other reasons, SPS’ own decisions in relation to the remission period for the inmate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: My point is, structurally, we need to ensure that the Commissioner is not unwittingly put in a position of conflict of interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I do appreciate, in a sense, this is an inherited issue because Parliament passed the amendment giving the Commissioner the power to defer issuing the remission order by 14 days in 2014.

sections.label: ex-offenders perform at NDP 2022
sections.summary: The speaker asks that talented ex-offenders be allowed to perform at NDP 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Please allow our talented ex-offenders to perform at NDP 2022.

sections.label: Bill perspective and Work Release Scheme
sections.summary: The speech approaches the Bill from a perspective tried in other jurisdictions and previously through a Work Release Scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My speech will be approaching this Bill from that perspective.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is something that has been tried in other jurisdictions and it is not unknown here, since we previously had a Work Release Scheme.

sections.label: bank collaborations and electronic payment access
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether similar collaborations can be made with other banks and whether legal impediments exist for ex-prisoners accessing electronic payment platforms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can similar collaborations be made with other banks?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Also, may I confirm if there are any legal impediments for ex-prisoners who have successfully established bank accounts to obtaining access to electronic payment platforms on their account, such as for example, NETS or PayNow, which are pretty much a ubiquitous feature of modern life for most of us?

sections.label: US prison labour pay
sections.summary: A government-owned US manufacturer reportedly paid inmate labour between $0.23 and $1.15 per hour, with facilities operating 24 hours a day, and the Member asked whether such prison work is covered under the Employment Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the US, a government-owned manufacturer using inmate labour, reportedly paid between $0.23 to $1.15 per hour, with its facilities operating 24 hours a day.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I would also like to ask the Minister of State, whether such prison work is covered under the Employment Act.

sections.label: Inmate scheme eligibility review
sections.summary: The SPS will assess all eligible inmates and refer them to an independent advisory committee, but there appears to be no appeal or review mechanism if an inmate is found not eligible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: MHA's press release, and I believe the hon Minister of State repeated this in his Second Reading speech, suggests the latter and specifies that the SPS will assess all eligible inmates and refers them to an independent advisory committee if they are assessed to be eligible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But there does not appear to be any appeal mechanism or review mechanism if the SPS decides that an inmate is not eligible for such a scheme and hence is not referred to the independent committee.

sections.label: Five-year recidivism rates
sections.summary: The five-year recidivism rate for the 2011 to 2015 release cohorts was 43.1%, 43.2%, 41%, 41.3% and 41.7% respectively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Based on the reply to a Parliamentary Question for MHA that I filed in August last year, the five-year recidivism rate and – before I continue I should state that I think the hon Minister of State and the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai did refer to the two-year recidivism rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But the five-year recidivism rate for the 2011 to 2015 release cohorts, were 43.1%, 43.2%, 41%, 41.3% and 41.7% respectively.

sections.label: Minister's regulation-making power
sections.summary: Section 84(2) gives the Minister for Home Affairs power to make regulations imposing a condition on prescribed persons to give an undertaking not to publish or disseminate certain information from communications with an inmate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Section 84(2) gives the Minister for Home Affairs power to make regulations to impose a condition on prescribed persons to give an undertaking that it will not publish or disseminate or cause to be published or disseminated any information contained in any communication with an inmate that may affect the security or good order of the prison or incite the commission of any offence before they are allowed to visit or communicate with an inmate.

sections.label: Penalties for breaching undertaking
sections.summary: The Member asked whether the Government can specify the penalties associated with a prescribed person breaching the undertaking.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can the Government also specify the penalties associated with such a prescribed person breaching the undertaking?

sections.label: Withholding prisoner correspondence
sections.summary: This provision and section 127A allow letters to prisoners to be withheld if they affect prison security or good order, and this provision adds withholding or redacting correspondence that could incite an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Both this provision and section 127A provide that letters to prisoners may be withheld if they affect the security or good order of prisons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But this provision also goes further in providing for a new category of reasons whereby correspondence can be withheld, that is, withholding or redacting correspondence that could incite the commission of any offence.

sections.label: Information targeted and genuine grievances
sections.summary: Asks whether actions target information in footnote 5 and seeks assurance that genuine grievances posing no security risk are unaffected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Will actions under this provision target the kinds of information detailed in footnote 5 to the MHA press release, which seem very directly related to the commission of offences?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Would the Ministry provide the assurance that information on genuine grievances a person may have that do not pose security risks would not be affected?

sections.label: Withheld lawyer correspondence notification
sections.summary: Suggests that when inmate-lawyer correspondence is withheld, the prisoner and lawyer should at least be told.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, I think that if correspondence between an inmate and his lawyer is withheld, at the very least that fact should be conveyed to the prisoner and his/her lawyer.

sections.label: Intercepting prisoner communication for AGC
sections.summary: Asks whether the Government can intercept prisoner communication and convey contents to AGC for legal advantage, even if unrelated to an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Lastly, I would also like to ask if, under this provision, the Government can intercept prisoner communication and convey part or all of the contents of the same to AGC to confer a legal advantage on the latter, even if it is unrelated to the commission of an offence as described in the language of the provision and in the MHA press release.

sections.label: Prisons Amendment Bill amendments categories
sections.summary: The Prisons (Amendment) Bill proposes two main categories of amendments, including enhancing community corrections for rehabilitation and reintegration.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The Prisons (Amendment) Bill proposes mainly two categories of amendments, including enhancing community corrections for better rehabilitation and reintegration outcomes.

sections.label: 2013 study on education and recidivism
sections.summary: A 2013 study found American inmates in educational programmes had 13% better employment chances and were 43% less likely to recidivate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: To give an example, a 2013 study showed how participation in educational programmes increased the chances of employment of American inmates upon their release by 13% compared to their peers and are 43% less likely to recidivate compared to those who did not undergo the programme.

sections.label: Recidivism and community rehabilitation figures
sections.summary: The two-year recidivism rate nearly halved in 20 years to about 22%, and community-based rehabilitation numbers rose 42% from 2019 to 2020.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Our two-year recidivism rate has almost halved in 20 years to reach approximately 22%, although the five-year recidivism rate is higher.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: From 2019 to 2020, there was a 42% increase in the number of inmates who underwent community-based rehabilitation and the completion rates for these programmes were over 90%.

sections.label: Ex-offender education study findings
sections.summary: A SACA study found ex-offenders' criminal records hindered employment, and many jobs paid less than their qualifications warranted.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The Singapore After-Care Association (SACA) published a study on ex-offenders who had participated in their Education Support Programme and completed higher education post-release.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Respondents noted that their criminal record hindered them in all stages of employment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Of those that secured a job, many found that their positions and pay grade were less than commensurate with their educational qualifications.

sections.label: Inmate correspondence restrictions
sections.summary: Inmates' letters and emails are scrutinised, and they are limited to two letters or four emails monthly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Inmates’ correspondence with family members and friends are already subject to scrutiny and from my understanding, inmates are restricted to sending out two letters or up to four emails in a month.

sections.label: Employment Preparation Scheme welcomed
sections.summary: The Employment Preparation Scheme is described as a step in the right direction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: As such, The Employment Preparation Scheme (EmPS) is a step in the right direction.

sections.label: Conditions for potential employers
sections.summary: Potential employers should meet conditions or give SPS a training plan and remuneration schedule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Potential employers should meet certain conditions, or provide a specific training plan and remuneration schedule to the Singapore Prison Service, or SPS.

sections.label: New Zealand Release to Work
sections.summary: New Zealand's Release to Work Programme requires potential employers to satisfy criteria before placement with rehabilitating inmates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: New Zealand’s Release to Work Programme requires potential employers to satisfy a set of criteria, before they can be considered for placement with inmates undergoing rehabilitation.

sections.label: Clause 59M prohibitions scope
sections.summary: The prohibitions in clause 59M (2) do not expressly mention vice activities, aside from drugs and alcohol.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: With regards to clause 59M (2), the prohibitions in the said clause do not expressly mention vice activities, aside from drugs and alcohol.

sections.label: De-identifying EmPS participants
sections.summary: De-identifying EmPS participants gives them a fair chance at rehabilitation without societal stigma, and asks how victims' needs and rejection cases are handled.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: De-identifying EmPS participants gives them a fair chance at rehabilitation, to prove themselves without societal stigma.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Correspondingly, how will the Ministry seek to protect the needs of victims of crime and to navigate situations whereby halfway through the EmPS, a co-worker or classmate rejects the presence of the participating inmate?

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Can the Ministry share how many cases of deferment to conduct punishments have occurred in the past?

sections.label: Attracting genuine employers
sections.summary: To be more effective and benefit more former inmates, it needs to attract genuine employers keen to help ex-offenders and grow their businesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: For it to be more effective and benefit more former inmates, it needs to attract genuine employers – employers who are keen to help ex-offenders and at the same time, employ them to grow their businesses.

sections.label: Onboarding employers and workplaces
sections.summary: Onboarding more eligible employers and workplaces is hoped to increase acceptance of ex-offenders, supporting a Bill amending the Prisons Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: As we onboard more eligible employers and workplaces, I am hopeful that this will help increase the acceptance of ex-offenders into our society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: I stand in support of the Bill, which seeks to amend the Prisons Act to enhance community corrections and facilitate better operations and administration of the Singapore Prison Service (SPS).

sections.label: Replacing WRS with EmPS
sections.summary: Replacing the WRS with the EmPS will help reduce skills mismatch and ease ex-offenders' transition into society through good employment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: The proposed replacement of the WRS with the EmPS, will help reduce this skills mismatch and ease the transition of our ex-offenders into society through good employment.

sections.label: Job openings and excluded jobs
sections.summary: In September 2021 there were 209 job openings per 100 unemployed persons, but some jobs are automatically excluded from ex-offenders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: In September 2021, there were 209 job openings for every 100 unemployed persons in Singapore, according to data from the MOM.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: There is certainly space for us to do more to help place ex-offenders into manpower-deficient sectors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: However, certain jobs such as those in the security sector, or those that require approval from the Police to enter restricted areas such as our ports and the airport, are automatically excluded from ex-offenders due to their past convictions.

sections.label: CBP recidivism rates
sections.summary: Offenders on CBPs in 2016 to 2018 had a 16% recidivism rate versus 26% for those not on such programmes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As reported by The Straits Times, offenders placed on CBPs in the period 2016 to 2018 had a 16% recidivism rate as compared to 26% for offenders who were not on such programmes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Of course, it also bears stating that – as mentioned by the Minister of State and several hon Members who spoke before me – Singapore already has one of the lowest recidivism rates in the world and the current two-year recidivism rate of 22% is one of the lowest we have ever had, although the five-year rates are higher.

sections.label: Elderly inmates and ex-offenders
sections.summary: Convicted inmates aged 51 and above rose 70% from 2012 to 2017, those 60 and above tripled, and elderly ex-offenders struggled to find work after release.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Already, we can see based on data from the SPS that the number of convicted inmates aged 51 and above in the period 2012 to 2017 has increased by 70% and the number of inmates aged 60 years and above tripled over the same period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A study by the Singapore After-Care Association published in December 2018 found that elderly ex-offenders had difficulties finding employment upon their release.

sections.label: Singapore recidivism rate
sections.summary: Singapore's two-year recidivism rate is 22.1%, one of the lowest in the world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Singapore's two-year recidivism rate of 22.1% is one of the lowest in the world.

sections.label: WRS inmates and absconder rate
sections.summary: The question asks for the current number and percentage of inmates allowed to leave prisons under WRS and the absconder rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: What is the current number and percentage of inmates that are allowed to leave prisons under WRS and what is the absconder rate?

sections.label: SPS officers' investigative powers
sections.summary: The amendments give SPS officers powers to obtain documents or information from third parties to investigate breaches of conditions by supervisees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: While we do want more of our inmates to be better prepared and ultimately reintegrate back to society, we must also be mindful not to tolerate any breaches of conditions by supervisees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Hence, the amendments also provide SPS officers with powers to obtain documents or information from third parties and this will be a required amendment to assist our SPS officers to investigate and make inquiries into breaches of conditions by supervisees.

sections.label: EmPS and SkillsFuture Credit
sections.summary: The question asks whether inmates placed on EmPS can use their SkillsFuture Credit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Can inmates placed on EmPS use their SkillsFuture Credit too?

sections.label: FITRAH support and amendments support
sections.summary: FITRAH by MUIS with M3 provides integrated support for offenders and families, and the speaker supports the amendments while listing conditions for their effectiveness.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Programmes such as FITRAH (Family and Inmates Through Care Assistance Haven) by the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) together with M3 aims to provide integrated and holistic support for offenders and their families – from in-care to aftercare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: (In English): In conclusion, Mdm Deputy Speaker, overall, I am in support of the amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: However, for it to be effective, we need to ensure that SPS is adequately resourced; we have good quality training and trained training providers to enable the inmates to reintegrate through meaningful employment; we have strong support from employers in the right industries; we can ensure the inmate's family is supported, advised and counselled so that they can be the pillar of support for the inmates to reintegrate back to society; lastly and perhaps most crucially, we need to continue our efforts in getting society to accept these individuals who are intending to turn over a new leaf and be contributing members of our society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: That being said, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I am in support of the amendments to the Bill.

sections.label: 14-day release eligibility remand
sections.summary: New section 59L makes a prisoner eligible for release for employment preparation after serving at least 14 days, and asks if remand time counts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The new section 59L provides that a prisoner is eligible to be released for employment preparation if the prisoner has served not less than 14 days.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can Minister clarify whether this 14-day period includes any time that has been spent in remand?

sections.label: Aggravated prison offence misconduct
sections.summary: Carrying out a gross act of misconduct or insubordination is an aggravated prison offence, but it is unclear whether prejudicial acts are less severe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It is an aggravated prison offence to carry out any “gross act of misconduct or insubordination”.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: But it is not clear that acts that are prejudicial to the good order or discipline in the prison are any less severe than acts of gross misconduct or insubordination.

sections.label: Assault and self-harm offences
sections.summary: Asks why aggravated or repeated assault on another prisoner, or wilfully causing oneself illness, injury or disability outside prison under the scheme is no longer a prison offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can Minister also clarify why it is no longer a prison offence for a prisoner to carry out aggravated or repeated assault on any other prisoner, or wilfully causing themselves any illness, injury, or disability if a prisoner is outside of prison under the scheme?

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Every year, more than 10,000 ex-offenders complete their sentences and are released.

sections.label: Section 59L(a) eligibility
sections.summary: Under section 59L(a) of the Bill, an inmate is eligible for the scheme after serving at least 14 days of their sentence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: At section 59L(a) of the Bill, an inmate is eligible for the scheme when they have served at least 14 days of their sentence.

sections.label: YRSG employment assistance
sections.summary: YRSG assists over 2,000 inmates yearly with employment before release, and since 2018 e2i has helped about 1,000 ex-offenders through training and job matching.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Every year, YRSG assists more than 2,000 inmates with employment before release.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: For example, since 2018, e2i has worked with YRSG to assist approximately 1,000 ex-offenders by developing training programmes and providing job matching opportunities for this pool of workers.

sections.label: Family issues and home leave
sections.summary: Inmates with family issues may inform their Reintegration Officer for joint sessions, but those without strong family support will not progress to home leave phases.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: If an inmate faces any family issue, he may inform his Reintegration Officer who can arrange joint sessions involving the inmate, family members and the Reintegration Officer, to resolve the issue.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: However, inmates assessed to be without strong family support will not progress to the home leave phases.

sections.label: In-camp and home leave phases
sections.summary: In-camp and weekend home leave phases each last two to four months on average, followed by long home leave until release for suitable inmates.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: On average, the duration of the in-camp and weekend home leave phases ranges from two to four months each; followed by the long home leave phase for suitable inmates, for the remaining period until they are released.

sections.label: EmPS and Second Schedule offence
sections.summary: For EmPS, an inmate is not automatically disqualified just because he committed an offence in the Second Schedule.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: For EmPS, an inmate is not automatically disqualified just because he committed an offence in the Second Schedule.

sections.label: EmPS supervision and conditions
sections.summary: Inmates on EmPS are under SPS close supervision and must comply with strict conditions like electronic tagging, curfew and reporting to mitigate re-offending risk.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: If emplaced on EmPS, the inmates will be under SPS’ close supervision.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: They will need to comply with strict conditions, such as electronic tagging, curfew and reporting to mitigate the risk of re-offending.

sections.label: 14-day period excludes remand
sections.summary: The 14-day period does not include time spent in remand.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: The 14-day period does not include time spent in remand.

sections.label: EmPS prohibited places
sections.summary: Inmates on EmPS are prohibited from patronising places of ill-repute such as brothels, nightclubs and massage parlours, among others.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Inmates on EmPS will be prohibited from patronising places of ill-repute, such as brothels, nightclubs and massage parlours, among others.

sections.label: Employers partnering YRSG
sections.summary: Currently, over 5,600 employers partner YRSG to offer jobs to ex-offenders.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Currently, there are over 5,600 employers partnering YRSG to offer jobs to ex-offenders.

sections.label: YRSG training academies in prison
sections.summary: YRSG has partnered three organisations to set up precision engineering, media skills and logistics training academies in prison.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: To date, YRSG has partnered the Singapore Precision Engineering and Technology Association, Mediacorp, Singapore Logistics Association to set up precision engineering, media skills and logistics training academies in prison.

sections.label: JGI for ex-offender hires
sections.summary: Employers who hired ex-offenders through YRSG, ISCOS or SPS-engaged halfway houses automatically receive the JGI of up to $36,000.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Employers who hired ex-offenders through YRSG, the Industrial and Services Co-operative Society (ISCOS), or halfway houses engaged by SPS, will automatically receive the JGI of up to $36,000 for these hires.

sections.label: Criteria for partnering employers
sections.summary: YRSG requires partnering employers to meet criteria including fair employment practices, CPF contributions, supportive work practices and market-relevant salaries.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: YRSG requires partnering employers to fulfil certain criteria.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: These include abiding by fair employment practices, providing CPF contributions for employees, adopting supportive work practices and providing market-relevant salaries, including aligning salaries with the Progressive Wage Model.

sections.label: Unfair treatment of employees
sections.summary: If an employer is reported to treat employees unfairly because of their criminal records, YRSG may pause or cease the partnership.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: If an employer is reported to treat employees unfairly because of their criminal records, YRSG may pause, or even cease the partnership with the employer.

sections.label: Remuneration into inmates' accounts
sections.summary: The employers will credit the remuneration directly into the inmates' bank accounts.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: The employers will credit the remuneration directly into the inmates' bank accounts.

sections.label: Training costs for inmates
sections.summary: Inmates attending YRSG-arranged training courses pay nothing, with a 70% to 90% national subsidy and YRSG bearing the rest.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Inmates who attend training courses arranged by YRSG are not required to pay for the training.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: There is a national subsidy of 70% to 90% for skills training provided by ATOs and CET Centres, and the remaining cost will be borne by YRSG.

sections.label: Bursary and education support
sections.summary: An inmate may apply for the Yellow Ribbon Fund STAR Bursary or the Singapore After-Care Association's Education Support Programme to support his education.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: If need be, he may apply for the Yellow Ribbon Fund STAR Bursary or the Education Support Programme offered by the Singapore After-Care Association to support his education.

sections.label: Digital skills training pathways
sections.summary: YRSG is developing tiered training pathways for inmates to gain digital skills, starting in the second quarter of 2022.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: YRSG is also developing tiered training pathways for inmates to gain digital skills, which will commence in the second quarter of 2022.

sections.label: Wrist-worn tracking device
sections.summary: SPS is currently developing a tracking device resembling a digital watch that can be worn on the wrist.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: SPS is currently developing a tracking device that resembles a digital watch which can be worn on the wrist.

sections.label: Work Release Scheme statistics
sections.summary: About 200 inmates are emplaced on the WRS yearly, with 101 on the scheme as of end 2021, and a 15% two-year recidivism rate for 2014-2018 completers.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: About 200 inmates are emplaced on the WRS yearly.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: As of end 2021, there were 101 inmates on the scheme, forming about 3% of the convicted inmate population.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: In 2021, the number of inmates who absconded during their WRS averaged about two per month, or which is about 1.3% of the WRS population per month.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Based on the latest data, for inmates released from 2014 to 2018, the average two-year recidivism rate of inmates who had completed the WRS is 15% as compared to 24% for the general inmate population.

sections.label: Deferring remission order issuance
sections.summary: The Commissioner of Prisons' power to defer issuing a remission order addresses operational issues, has worked well, and can be retained.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: He said there could be a situation where the Commissioner is asked to consider deferring the issuance of a remission order because there is insufficient time for the carrying out the corporal punishment on an inmate because of, amongst others, SPS' own decisions in relation to the remission period for the inmate.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: This is because the restoration and forfeiture of an inmate’s remission will not result in him serving less than two-thirds of his imprisonment sentence before remission is granted.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: And because inmates must serve two-thirds of their imprisonment sentence before they can be considered for release under the CRS, this situation will not arise.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: On the more fundamental question on whether the Commissioner of Prisons should continue to have the power to defer issuing the remission order, from our perspective, this arrangement to address operational issues has been working well and can be retained.

sections.label: Fourteen-day appeal period
sections.summary: The 14-day period gives individuals, not limited to inmates, sufficient time to consider appealing against a judgement, order or sentence.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: The 14-day period is given to allow individuals, not limited to inmates alone, to have sufficient time to think if they wish to appeal against a judgement, order or sentence.

sections.label: Caning and release timing
sections.summary: SPS says inmates will be caned at the earliest possible instance and released soonest thereafter, with no release deferred beyond what is necessary.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: SPS will exercise such powers judiciously and no inmate’s release will be deferred by more than what is necessary for carrying out the Court-ordered punishment.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: This means that the inmate concerned will be caned at the earliest possible instance and released soonest thereafter.

sections.label: Inmates' correspondence controls, no exemptions
sections.summary: The new provision on control of inmates' correspondence lets SPS regulate information affecting prison security or inciting offences, with no exemption for any group including lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: On whether the new provisions on controls to inmates' correspondence will have specific carve-outs for any groups, including lawyers, the new provision on control of inmates' correspondence is intended to enable SPS to regulate information that affects the security or good order of the prison or incites the commission of a new offence.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: We do not intend to exempt any group or persons, including lawyers, from this provision.

sections.label: Employment Act for EmPS inmates
sections.summary: Inmates working in the community under the EmPS have a contract of service and employer-employee relationship, so they are protected under the Employment Act.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: He also asked if the Employment Act applies to inmates working on the EmPS.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: So, when they are working in the community, they have a contract of service and share an employer-employee relationship with the company and thus, they are protected under the Employment Act.

sections.label: Recidivism rate and EmPS programmes
sections.summary: The five-year recidivism rate is about twice the two-year rate, and new programmes like the EmPS aim to improve it with support from the House, families and community.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: Mr Perera mentioned about the five-year recidivism rate, which is about two times higher than the two-year recidivism rate.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: We agree that there is room for improvement, that is why we want to implement new programmes such as the EmPS to improve this rate.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: However, SPS and YSRG cannot do this alone over the longer timeframe.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
sentences.text: We need even stronger support from this House, families, the community and an accepting society.

sections.label: Assurance on inmate-lawyer correspondence
sections.summary: An MP asks the Minister of State to assure that inmate correspondence with lawyers or others would never be relayed to third parties like the AGC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: In fact, all my points and questions have been raised, except one.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I just wanted to come back to one question I had at the end of my speech, which is on the powers that the Government now has to interdict correspondence or redact or review correspondence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I just wanted to ask for the Minister of State's assurance that whatever correspondence that an inmate has with his or her lawyer or even with other persons – that information, under our current laws and regulations, could never be and would not be used and relayed on to third parties, such as the AGC, for example, to confer some kind of legal advantage in the proceedings that follow.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I just wanted to get that assurance that that is not something that could possibly happen right now.
